title: Inflation, currency depreciation, and the sovereign-bank nexus: a quantile panel analysis of banking fragility across eight African economies
venue: Future Business Journal
summary: Abstract Banking sector fragility in Africa has re-emerged as a first-order macro-financial concern amid a decade of currency depreciation episodes, elevated and volatile inflation, and mounting sovereign debt stress. title: Dividend signals, market imperfections and speculative bubble dynamics in an emerging market: Empirical evidence from the Moroccan stock market
venue: Cogent Business & Management
summary: This study examines the relationship between dividend policy and speculative dynamics in an emerging stock market. Using a balanced panel of 33 firms listed on the Casablanca Stock Exchange over 2003–2025, the analysis combines GSADF/BSADF procedures with econometric models of three dimensions: entry into an explosive state, speculative intensity, and exit from that state. Dividend policy is measured by the dividend-payment decision, Payout ratio, and Dividend Yield. The results reveal no systematic and robust association between these three measures and any of the speculative dimensions examined. This conclusion remains broadly unchanged when dividend variables are lagged, alternative definitions of the intensity indicator are considered, its dynamics are accounted for, and the GSADF/BSADF specification is varied. Accordingly, none of the three hypotheses receives robust empirical support. Although dividends may retain informational, disciplinary, or shareholder-remuneration functions, they do not, on their own, constitute a sufficiently stable determinant of speculative dynamics. Given the annual data and the constructed nature of the intensity indicator, the results should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects. The study contributes to bridging the literature on dividend policy with research on speculative behavior in emerging markets.

title: When rules become clear: capital market reactions to Hong Kong's Stablecoin Ordinance
venue: Frontiers in Political Science
summary: This study examines capital market reactions to the gazettal of Hong Kong's Stablecoin Ordinance. title: The Scaling of Social Innovations in Africa and Beyond
venue: AIB Insights
summary: Scaling social innovations (SI) requires international networks to enhance legitimacy, secure funding, and maximize impacts that are measured beyond financial performance. The dual logic of managing revenues and impact with multiple stakeholders makes this scaling process more complex than profit-generating business models. Our observations of how SIs internationalize are based on two longitudinal cases of SIs in Africa – M-PESA, a Kenya-based firm, and Kiva, a USA-based company operating in Africa – which reveal the role of founder’s international networks in social impact scaling. We present a typology of SI scaling, future research questions for scholarship, and actionable insights to social entrepreneurs.

venue: International Review of Economics & Finance
summary: This study reassesses the usefulness of the Beneish Model as a financial statement fraud-risk screening tool in an emerging-market setting using evidence from 872 companies listed on the Stock Exchange of Thailand during 2013–2022. title: Systemic shocks and firm-level stock performance: evidence from Vietnam
venue: Cogent Economics & Finance
summary: This study investigates the impact of the COVID-19 lockdown on stock market performance in an emerging-market context, with particular emphasis on Vietnam. Specifically, the study examines whether firm-specific characteristics, including leverage, ownership structure, sector classification and market capitalization, moderate the effects of the lockdown on stock returns. The analysis employs a panel dataset of 375 firms listed on the Ho Chi Minh City Stock Exchange using daily observations from 30 January to 15 April 2020, covering both the pre-lockdown and nationwide lockdown periods. The analysis uses complementary event-study and panel-regression approaches (OLS, fixed effects, random effects and GLS) to examine market-wide responses and firm-level heterogeneity. The findings indicate that the lockdown announcement generated positive cumulative abnormal returns, suggesting that investors responded favorably to Vietnam’s rapid containment measures. However, the impact varied significantly across firms: highly leveraged firms and financial companies experienced relatively weaker stock performance, whereas state-owned enterprises and larger firms demonstrated greater resilience. These findings contribute to the literature on crisis-driven market behavior by highlighting the importance of firm-level heterogeneity in shaping stock market responses to systemic shocks and provide practical implications for investors, corporate managers and policymakers in emerging economies.

title: EARNINGS QUALITY, FIRM LIFE CYCLE, AND OWNERSHIP STRUCTURE: EVIDENCE FROM AN EMERGING MARKET
source: International Journal of Business and Society
venue: International Journal of Business and Society
summary: Using a sample of 351 non-financial firms listed on the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange from 2010 to 2023, this study investigates the impact of firm life cycle stages and ownership structure on the reliability and quality of reported earnings. Feasible generalized least squares regression analysis was employed to test the proposed relationships. An inverted U-shaped association was found between a firm’s life-cycle stage and earnings quality. Firms experience lower earnings quality in the introduction and decline stages due to lower profits, market fluctuation, and stakeholder pressure. In contrast, in the growth and maturity stages, firms witness earnings quality growth as a result of improved controlling and monitoring systems and higher revenue cash flows, which enhance the stability and reliability of profits. In terms of ownership structure, the empirical results indicated that state and foreign ownership positively and significantly influence earnings quality, whereas CEO ownership has no statistically significant impact. This study extends the existing earnings quality literature by providing empirical evidence on its key determinants in the Vietnamese market and offers practical implications for investors, policymakers, and financial managers seeking to mitigate earnings manipulation risks and improve investment decision-making.

title: Withholding-while-Giving: Safaricom, the State and Parastatal Cohabitation
venue: Ethnos
summary: This paper develops an account of parastatal governance, in which putatively distinct organizational forms – private corporation and public state – cohabitate. It does so through Safaricom, Kenya's largest firm. Known for telecommunications and mobile money services, Safaricom does much more than commerce. It is a chief promulgator of patriotism and is expected by Kenyans to provide what elsewhere might be considered ‘public goods’: famine relief, schooling, boreholes. Much like Serres's attention to the ambiguities of l'hôte in The Parasite, Safaricom occupies a zone of indeterminacy, neither clearly host nor guest, and is the object of welcoming entreaty and anxious resentment. To illustrate, the article examines two linked institutions: a charitable foundation and the legal and fiduciary devices that fund its initiatives. This builds on the anthropology of corporate social responsibility by demonstrating how legal trusts and the management of financial interests create a situation of both ‘with holding’ and ‘giving’.

title: Reassessing SEBI Regulations: Balancing Investor Protection, Market Integrity, and Regulatory Innovation in India's Securities Market
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The growth of the securities market in India has had a material impact on the development process of the Indian economy by enabling capital formation, enhancing the financing of corporations, and offering wider investment avenues. While on one hand, it has made considerable contributions towards this objective, the explosive growth of the market has simultaneously opened the floodgates for complex variants of insider trading, fraudulent transactions, corporate failures, and technological vulnerabilities that pose a daunting task for effective regulation. SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India), set up under the SEBI Act, 1992, is a cornerstone in confronting these issues with its myriad regulations concerning market functioning, disclosure requirements and investors. This article critiques the development of the SEBI framework, analyses its efficacy in regulating markets, looks at landmark judicial interventions, and highlights emerging threats due to the new trends in financial instruments. Thus, although SEBI has established a strong framework for promoting India's capital markets, the emphasis will need to be on flexibility and preparedness to meet new technological challenges and also on the need for prudent enforcement so that the quest for market efficiency does not undermine investor interests. Keywords: SEBI, Securities Regulation, Investor Protection, Corporate Governance, Insider Trading, Capital Markets.

title: The Sovereign-Bank Diabolic Loop and ESBies
venue: American Economic Review
summary: We propose a simple model of the sovereign-bank diabolic loop, and establish four results. First, the diabolic loop can be avoided by restricting banks' domestic sovereign exposures relative to their equity. Second, equity requirements can be lowered if banks only hold senior domestic sovereign debt. Third, such requirements shrink even further if banks only hold the senior tranche of an internationally diversified sovereign portfolio--known as ESBies in the euro-area context. Finally, ESBies generate more safe assets than domestic debt tranching alone; and, insofar as the diabolic loop is defused, the junior tranche generated by the securitization is itself risk-free.
